byTheNumbers.title: The year in numbers
byTheNumbers.standfirst: About 436 million people, nine in ten of them in villages, a quarter of them able to read, and a baby had a one-in-seven chance of dying in its first year.

items.title: How many Indians
items.summary: India's population was about 436 million in 1960; the census of 1961 counted a little over 439 million.

sources.label: World Bank, World Development Indicators: Population, total
Our World in Data: Population (UN World Population Prospects, HYDE)

items.title: Life expectancy at birth
items.summary: A newborn in 1960 could expect to live about 46 years.

sources.label: World Bank, World Development Indicators: Life expectancy at birth, total (years)
Our World in Data: Life expectancy (UN World Population Prospects and other series)

items.title: Who could read
items.summary: At the 1961 census about a quarter to 28 percent of people could read and write, 34 to 40 percent of men and 13 to 15 percent of women.

items.title: Town and village
items.summary: About 18 percent of Indians lived in towns and cities.

sources.label: World Bank, World Development Indicators: Urban population (% of total)

items.title: Infant deaths
items.summary: About 150 of every 1,000 babies died before their first birthday.

sources.label: World Bank, World Development Indicators: Mortality rate, infant (per 1,000 live births)

sensitivity.note: This item concerns the deaths of infants.

items.title: Births per woman
items.summary: The fertility rate was 5.9 births per woman.

sources.label: World Bank, World Development Indicators: Fertility rate, total (births per woman)

foodAndKitchen.title: Food and the kitchen
foodAndKitchen.standfirst: India imported large amounts of wheat from the US under PL-480 agreements to cover shortfalls.

items.title: Imported wheat
items.summary: India imported large amounts of wheat from the US under PL-480 agreements to cover shortfalls.

items.title: Vanaspati ghee
items.summary: Vanaspati, sold in tins as a cheaper substitute for ghee, was widely used in cooking.

items.title: India Coffee House
items.summary: The Indian Coffee Workers' Co-operative opened the first India Coffee House chain outlets in the 1950s, with waiters in turbans.

items.title: Kerosene stoves
items.summary: Kerosene and Primus stoves were spreading in towns, while villages still cooked on wood and dung.

clothingAndStyle.title: What people wore
clothingAndStyle.standfirst: The bandhgala-style jacket, linked with Nehru, became formal wear for politicians and officials.

items.title: The Nehru jacket
items.summary: The bandhgala-style jacket, linked with Nehru, became formal wear for politicians and officials.

items.title: Mill cloth and khadi
items.summary: Mills made most of the cloth sold, and khadi was promoted by the Khadi and Village Industries Commission set up in 1957.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Khadi and Village Industries Commission

items.title: Bata shoes
items.summary: Bata sold mass-made shoes, with a factory at Batanagar near Calcutta.

workAndWages.title: Work and wages
workAndWages.standfirst: The government built steel plants at Bhilai, Rourkela and Durgapur under the Second Five-Year Plan (1956-61).

items.title: Steel plants of the Second Plan
items.summary: The government built steel plants at Bhilai, Rourkela and Durgapur under the Second Five-Year Plan (1956-61).

items.title: Minimum Wages Act
items.summary: The Minimum Wages Act of 1948 let governments fix minimum pay for listed jobs.

items.title: Bombay's dabbawalas
items.summary: Dabbawalas carried home-cooked lunches to office workers in Bombay by train and bicycle.

schoolAndChildhood.title: Growing up
schoolAndChildhood.standfirst: IIT Kharagpur (1951), Bombay (1958), Madras (1959) and Kanpur (1959) were set up with foreign help.

items.title: The first IITs
items.summary: IIT Kharagpur (1951), Bombay (1958), Madras (1959) and Kanpur (1959) were set up with foreign help.

items.title: Meals at school in Madras
items.summary: Chief Minister Kamaraj began serving free midday meals in schools in Madras state in the 1950s to keep poor children in class.

items.title: Free schooling as a goal
items.summary: Article 45 of the Constitution asked the state to provide free and compulsory education to age 14 by 1960, a target that was missed.

gettingAround.title: Getting around
gettingAround.standfirst: Air India began flights to New York in 1960.

items.title: Air India to New York
items.summary: Air India began flights to New York in 1960.

gettingAround.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced 1960 railway or bus fares, or journey times.

keepingInTouch.title: Keeping in touch
keepingInTouch.standfirst: The radio was licensed, and its second national channel carried advertisements.

items.title: A licence for the radio
items.summary: In 1956 a minister told the Rajya Sabha that the radio licence fee had been raised from Rs 10 to Rs 15 because of administrative costs.

sources.label: Rajya Sabha debates, 3 May 1956: radio licence fee (question)

items.title: Advertising on the air
items.summary: Commercials were introduced on the Vividh Bharati service in 1957 on an experimental basis; its mix of film music, skits and short plays was meant to draw listeners from Radio Ceylon.

keepingInTouch.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced 1960 postal, telegram or telephone figures.

healthAndMedicine.title: Health and medicine
healthAndMedicine.standfirst: Smallpox was still common, and India accounted for most of the world's cases.

items.title: Smallpox
items.summary: A table in a 1962 newspaper lists about 31,052 attacks and 7,871 deaths from smallpox in India in 1960, down from about 106,500 attacks in 1958.

sources.label: Himalayan Times, 1962 (Heidelberg digital library): smallpox attacks and deaths table

sensitivity.note: This item describes deaths from disease.

items.title: A world share
items.summary: In the early 1960s India accounted for nearly 60 percent of the reported smallpox cases in the world, and the national eradication programme began in 1961-62.

sources.label: University of Michigan Library: Smallpox in India, pre-1972

sensitivity.note: This item describes deaths from disease.

leisureAndFun.title: Evenings, weekends and festivals
leisureAndFun.standfirst: K. Asif's epic Mughal-e-Azam was released in August 1960 and broke box-office records.

items.title: Mughal-e-Azam
items.summary: K. Asif's epic Mughal-e-Azam was released in August 1960 and broke box-office records.

items.title: Binaca Geetmala
items.summary: Ameen Sayani's countdown of film songs on Radio Ceylon, begun in 1952, was a weekly habit for listeners across India.

items.title: Milkha Singh at Rome
items.summary: Milkha Singh finished fourth in the 400 metres at the 1960 Rome Olympics, just missing a medal.

items.title: Cricket and the radio
items.summary: Test series against Pakistan in 1960-61 were followed on radio commentary.

spotlight.title: The new steel and project towns of the Five-Year Plans
spotlight.standfirst: Three steel plants built with Soviet, British and West German help began producing in 1959, and around them grew planned townships.

items.title: Three plants, three partners
items.summary: Under the Second Five-Year Plan Bhilai was built with the Soviet Union, Durgapur with Britain and Rourkela with West Germany.

items.title: Rourkela's first furnace
items.summary: President Rajendra Prasad opened Rourkela's first blast furnace, 'Parvati', on 3 February 1959, the plant's official founding date.

items.title: The villages that made way
items.summary: More than 30 villages were displaced for Rourkela, and about 13,000 to 16,000 people, mostly Adivasi, were resettled in colonies such as Jalda, Jhirpani and Bondamunda; the article says compensation was inadequate and promised jobs were often delayed.

sensitivity.note: This item concerns the forced resettlement of Adivasi families.

items.title: A township of 13 sectors
items.summary: Bhilai's planned township was laid out in 13 sectors, the plant provided subsidised education, healthcare and housing, and a once rural area became a cosmopolitan community with workers from across India.

items.title: Durgapur
items.summary: Durgapur's plant, set up with British help, began operating in 1959 for a planned one million tonnes of crude steel a year, in what grew into the largest industrial unit in West Bengal.

spotlight.scarcityNote: We could not find sourced wages, housing allotments or population for the steel towns in 1960.
